question.text: What is a 'ratio spread' and when might it be used?

answer.text: Buying fewer options at one strike and selling more options at a different strike (e.g., buy 1 ATM call, sell 2 OTM calls) — used when expecting moderate movement to the sold strike level, but with risk beyond that level
Buying equal numbers of calls and puts at different ratios to their premium
A spread where the ratio of premium to lot size is optimized
Trading options in a fixed ratio to futures contracts

explanation.text: The Logic: A ratio spread involves an unequal number of long and short options at different strikes on the same underlying and expiry. A typical ratio call spread is long 1 lower-strike call and short 2 higher-strike calls; maximum profit occurs at the short strike, the structure can often be entered for near-zero net premium, and beyond the short strike the extra naked short option creates significant directional risk. It is used when a trader expects only moderate movement up to the short strike. The Trap: The word "ratio" in this strategy refers to the unequal number of long versus short option contracts, not the ratio of premium to lot size, the ratio of premium to anything else, or the hedge ratio of options against a futures position. The naked short option(s) beyond the matched part create the asymmetric risk that defines the strategy. Note: The specific term "ratio spread" / "ratio call spread" was not located in the cited workbook pages (Currency p.101-p.114; IR p.167-p.184; Equity p.98-p.116), which cover vertical, horizontal, diagonal, straddle, strangle, covered call, collar, protective put, and butterfly strategies. The framing above is general options-strategy knowledge rather than a workbook citation.
